findings.title: Capability admission does not own the first executable boundary
findings.trigger: A Host profile combines executable candidate inspection with an enforcement record that should reject the Packet before Host-side code executes.
findings.impact: The driver layer performs process-backed discovery before the admission layer can enforce its invariant, so the supposedly central gate is bypassed by its own upstream dependency.
findings.evidence: The data flow is permission -> chooseExecutionDriver -> experimental disclosure -> enforcementAdmission -> fence. chooseExecutionDriver is not pure because identityProbes execute commands; therefore admission is not the first effect boundary.
findings.suggestion: Use the existing two concepts in the opposite order: make a pure capability/transport eligibility decision first, then run process-backed candidate attestation only for a route that could be admitted. Do not add a workflow engine or second Host registry.

findings.title: Installed policy is coupled to development-only qualification provenance
findings.trigger: The ultra-delegate Skill is installed from the npm package into another repository.
findings.impact: The runtime decision ships as constants while its named evidence remains only in this source checkout, so provenance ownership is ambiguous between product asset and project task evidence.
findings.evidence: HOST_ENFORCEMENT_QUALIFICATION embeds the local task attempt and receipt path. The package includes the Skill tree but excludes .ultra/evidence, and the record has no packaged immutable observation consumer.
findings.suggestion: Keep project task evidence as coordinator authority and, only if installed runtime diagnostics must cite it, ship one read-only redacted Skill-local evidence asset with the same digest. Avoid a database, registry or generated mirror.

findings.title: No-record Hosts are indistinguishable from positively admitted Hosts
findings.trigger: A later Step 1 controller calls enforcementAdmission for a Host whose legacy N=1 conformance passed but whose factory effect dimensions were never qualified.
findings.impact: The returned route is admitted with gate null and no explicit not-qualified state, so a new factory consumer could mistake legacy compatibility for D1 factory admission unless it adds another check.
findings.evidence: The no-record branch returns admitted and the unit test explicitly preserves that behavior for five Hosts. Current docs call it conformance-gated admission with no capability claim, and Step 1 is not yet implemented, so existing N=1 compatibility is not presently broken.
findings.suggestion: Before Step 1 consumes this API, expose the legacy/no-claim state distinctly or require the Supervisor Profile to demand an enforcement-qualified gate; do not globally disable existing N=1 delegation in this task.

positive_observations: The implementation reuses the existing Host profile and permission/result path rather than introducing a generic sandbox or orchestration subsystem.
Legacy N=1 compatibility is deliberately separated from a positive factory-enforcement claim in the maintained prose.
limitations: The no-record admission risk becomes blocking only when a Step 1 Supervisor consumes this API; it is retained as P2 under the current D1 scope.
